parole.significato: The name of the Cyrillic script letter А/а.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian а (a).

parole.significato: Belonging to or pertaining to a Bronze Age era culture from the Chuvash region of Russia.See Abashevo culture
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian Аба́шев (Abášev).

parole.significato: Synonym of Abaza.
parole.testo: From Russian абази́н (abazín).

parole.significato: Abkhazian: of or pertaining to Abkhazia, the Abkhazian people, or their language.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian абха́з (abxáz).

parole.significato: A hospital or hospital department that specializes in abortions.
parole.testo: From abort. Compare auditorium, vomitorium. Possibly a borrowing of Russian абортарий (abortarij) or its variant аборторий (abortorij).

parole.significato: A literary movement in early twentieth-century Russia, reacting against symbolism and concerned with greater immediacy…
parole.testo: From Russian акмеи́зм (akmeízm), from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Political warfare conducted by the Soviet or Russian government since the 1920s to advance foreign policy, including es…
parole.testo: Calque of Russian акти́вные мероприя́тия (aktívnyje meroprijátija)

parole.significato: Any natural herbal substance, such as ginseng, that is purported to assist the body to adapt to stress, and to exert a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian адаптоген (adaptogen), coined by Soviet toxicologist and pharmacologist Nikolai Lazarev. By surface analysis, adapt + -o- + -gen.

parole.significato: A hot, spicy but subtly flavoured paste often used to flavour food, mainly in the Caucasian regions of Abkhazia and Sam…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian аджи́ка (adžíka), from Abkhaz аџьыка (adžəkʼa); see there for more.

parole.significato: Of or relating to both Africa and Asia.
parole.testo: Blend of Afro- (prefix meaning ‘Africa’) + Asian, possibly a calque of Russian афрази́йский (afrazíjskij, “of, pertaining to, or being a language family spoken in northern Africa and southwest Asia”).

parole.significato: An administrative unit in the USSR, composed of an amalgamation of collective farms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian агрогород (agrogorod, “agronomic town”).

parole.significato: The Soviet-built 1947 Kalashnikov assault rifle or any similar rifle built to this design.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian АК-47 (AK-47), shortened from автома́т Кала́шникова 1947 (avtomát Kalášnikova 1947) (Kalashnikov's automatic rifle), from the name of the designer Mikhail Kalashnikov.

parole.significato: A case of vowel reduction in Slavic languages; the merger of pretonic non-high vowel phonemes (/o/, /e/ and /a/).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian а́канье (ákanʹje).

parole.significato: A trigonal-hexagonal scalenohedral steel gray mineral containing bismuth, lead, sulfur, and tellurium.
parole.testo: From Russian Алексеев (Aleksejev) + -ite, after the mine where it was found.

parole.significato: Of the Aleutian Islands, their inhabitants or their language.
parole.testo: From Russian алеу́т (aleút), probably from a native word, perhaps Aleut allíthuh (“community”) or Chukchi aliat (“island”).

parole.significato: Denoting a scope that included all of the Soviet Union rather than only one or several Republics of the Soviet Union.
parole.testo: Calque of Russian всесоюзный (vsesojuznyj): the conventionally standard English translation.

parole.significato: A trigonal-hexagonal scalenohedral mineral containing calcium, chlorine, hydrogen, manganese, niobium, oxygen, silicon,…
parole.testo: From Russian Аллуайв (Alluajv) + -ite, named for the mountain where it occurs.

parole.significato: caviar from the albino beluga
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian алма́з (almáz, “diamond”).

parole.significato: A Native American hostage taken by Russian colonists.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian амана́т (amanát, “hostage”), via a Turkic language from Arabic أَمَانَة (ʔamāna, “surety”).

parole.significato: Any of various hybrids of the white amur that were bred for aquatic weed control.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian аму́р (amúr), from an Ewenic language such as Solon amur (“river”). Doublet of Amur.

parole.significato: A triclinic-pinacoidal mineral containing calcium, hydrogen, iron, oxygen, and phosphorus.
parole.testo: From Russian Анапа (Anapa) + -ite, named for the town near where it was discovered.

parole.significato: The Soviet machinery of state bureaucratic administration, or a similar communistic structure.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian аппара́т (apparát, “apparatus, apparat”). Doublet of apparatus.

parole.significato: A member of the Soviet apparat; a Communist bureaucrat or agent.
parole.testo: From Russian аппара́тчик (apparátčik, “operator, apparatchik”), from аппара́т (apparát, “apparat, apparatus (of state)”) + suffix -чик (-čik).

parole.significato: The higher order of clergy in Russia, including metropolitans, archbishops, and bishops.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian архиере́й (arxijeréj), from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: In the Russian Empire, a person who farmed local rents or revenues.
parole.testo: From Russian аренда́тор (arendátor), from Latin arendator, arrendator, from arendare, arrendare (“to pay rent”), from arenda (“yearly rent”), from ad + renda (whence French rente, English rent). Compare arrentation and rent.

parole.significato: A murre or guillemot.
parole.testo: Ultimately onomatopoeic from the bird's cry, the name may have entered English via Russian; it is also used by the Aleuts.

parole.significato: An obsolete Russian length unit, equal to 71.12 centimeters, or 28 inches.
parole.testo: From Russian арши́н (aršín), from Ottoman Turkish آرشون / آرشین (arşın) (Turkish arşın).

parole.significato: A Russian or Soviet craftsmen's collective.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian артель (artelʹ).

parole.significato: A thick liquid residuum obtained in the distillation of Russian petroleum, much used as fuel.
parole.testo: From Russian оста́тки (ostátki), nominative and accusative plural of оста́ток (ostátok), meaning "remnants".

parole.significato: A title of Cossack and haidamak leaders of various kinds. The term was also used for the leader of a fisherman artel an…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian атама́н (atamán).

parole.significato: A planned city built to facilitate the construction and operation of a nuclear power plant or other nuclear facility in…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian атомгра́д (atomgrád), from а́том (átom, “atom”) + град (grad, “city”).

parole.significato: A village encampment in the Caucasus, Central Asia or the Southern Urals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian ау́л (aúl), from West (Kypchak) Turkic awul, awïl; compare Karachay-Balkar ауул (awul), Bashkir ауыл (awıl), Kazakh ауыл (awıl) and Turkish ağıl.

parole.significato: An Eastern European (especially Russian) grandmother.
parole.testo: From Russian бабу́ля (babúlja).

parole.significato: An Eastern European old woman.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian ба́бушка (bábuška, “grandmother”), from Old East Slavic бабушка (babuška, “grandmother, midwife”). First attested in the 1830s.

parole.significato: A freshwater sponge (genus Spongilla) formerly used to treat bruises, pleurisy, scrofula, etc.
parole.testo: From Russian бадя́га (badjága).

parole.significato: Small-scale peddlers or traders operating in the wake of economic and political collapse, often having been displaced f…
parole.testo: Calque of Russian мешочники (mešočniki), from the large sacks they often carried.

parole.significato: The parakeet auklet.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian белобрюшка (belobrjuška).

parole.significato: Support for Mikhail Bakunin respectively his propositions.
parole.testo: From his name + -ism, and borrowed directly or indirectly particularly from Russian бакуни́зм (bakunízm) in its shorter alternative form (the suffix -ин (-in) in his name has a tendency to be dropped).

parole.significato: Relating to, or supporting the revolutionary anarchism of Mikhail Bakunin
parole.testo: From Bakunin + -ist. parole.significato: A plucked stringed instrument with a triangular body, short neck and three strings, of Russian origin.
parole.testo: From Russian балала́йка (balalájka).

parole.significato: A type of steam bath, popular in Russia (and in some parts of Alaska as well).
parole.testo: From Russian ба́ня f (bánja). Doublet of bagnio, bain, and balaneion.

parole.significato: A traditional Russian dough ring, somewhat smaller than a bublik, but also thinner and drier.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian бара́нка (baránka).

parole.significato: An arc-shaped shifting sand dune comprising well-sorted (uniformly sized) sand.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Russian барха́н (barxán), from a Turkic language such as Kazakh барқан (barqan); further etymology unknown. The Russian word was first used in scientific literature in 1881 by the Russian zoologist and explorer Alexander von Middendorf (1815–1894).

parole.significato: Synonym of boyar.
parole.testo: From Russian ба́рин (bárin).

parole.significato: A regal Russian mantle or neckpiece made of gold, encrusted with diamonds and other gems.
parole.testo: From Russian барма (barma).

parole.significato: A purported zoophyte, half-animal and half-plant, said to grow in the form of a sheep.
parole.testo: Possibly a corruption of Russian баране́ц (baranéc, “species of club moss (genus Lycopodium)”, from бара́н (barán, “ram (male sheep)”) + -ец (-ec, diminutive suffix)).

parole.significato: An Aleutian underground dwelling.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian барабора (barabora), from Itelmen [Term?].

parole.significato: A high-pressure high-temperature apparatus usually used for growing or processing minerals, especially diamond.
parole.testo: Transliteration of the Russian БАРС (BARS), abbreviation for Беспрессовая Аппаратура высокого давления (press-free high-pressure setup).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a certain Turkic ethnic group that lives mostly in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan.
parole.testo: From Russian башки́р (baškír).

parole.significato: A protective cone-shaped hood with lappets for wrapping around the neck, used especially by Turks and Cossacks.
parole.testo: From Russian башлы́к (bašlýk), from Ottoman Turkish باشلق (başlık).

parole.significato: A rod or cane used for corporal punishment in Russia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian бато́г (batóg).

parole.significato: A type of chromatic button accordion developed in Russia in the early 20th century.
parole.testo: From Russian бая́н (baján); named after the 11th-century bard Boyan.

parole.significato: A roughly cone shaped rock formation, usually consisting of siltstone, peat or loam.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian байджара́х (bajdžaráx), from Yakut бадьараах (bajaraax).

parole.significato: The name of the Cyrillic script letter Б / б
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian бэ (bɛ).

parole.significato: A person who dresses in a manner that is not socially acceptable and is supposed to reject conventional norms of though…
parole.testo: Coined by American columnist Herb Caen in 1958. From beat (generation) + -nik (“person who exemplifies or endorses something”). Compare jazznik. parole.significato: A type of Russian heavy draft horse, originally from Voronezh guberniya on the Bityug river.
parole.testo: From the name of the Bityug river near Voronezh, ultimately from Russian битю́г (bitjúg), which is from Turkic.

parole.significato: A whale, Delphinapterus leucas, found in the Arctic Ocean.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian белу́га (belúga), from бе́лый (bélyj, “white”). In modern standard Russian, белу́га (belúga) denotes the fish Huso huso only, while белу́ха (belúxa) denotes the cetacean.

parole.significato: A type of large disposable ship that was used for timber-rafting along the rivers Volga and Kama from the end of the 16…
parole.testo: From Russian беляна (beljana).

parole.significato: The scientific study of birchbark manuscripts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian берестоло́гия (berestológija) from береста́ (berestá, “birchbark”) + -ло́гия (-lógija, suffix indicating the study of a particular subject).

parole.significato: An old Russian unit of weight, approximately 164 kilograms or 10 poods.
parole.testo: From Russian бе́рковец (bérkovec); derived from бе́рковеск (bérkovesk), Old East Slavic бьрковьскъ (bĭrkovĭskŭ, “of Birka”), ultimately Old Norse Birka, a port city in mediaeval Sweden.

parole.significato: Synonym of golden eagle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian бе́ркут (bérkut), itself a Turkic borrowing; ultimately from Proto-Turkic *bürküt.

parole.significato: A knee-length outer garment with a short stand-up collar, typical of Turkic, Mongolian and Caucasian peoples, similar t…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian бешме́т (bešmét), itself from Tatar бишмәт (bişmät).

parole.significato: A flat visorless sailor's cap.
parole.testo: From Russian бескозы́рка (beskozýrka).

parole.significato: A fundamental breakdown in the established norms of a society, due to its citizens no longer having a collective unders…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian беспреде́л (bespredél, “lawlessness; arbitrary rule”), from бес- (bes-, “without”) + преде́л (predél, “limit”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Zaum.
parole.testo: Blend of beyond + nonsense, coined to translate Russian зáумь (záumʹ), from за- (za-, “trans-, beyond”) + ум (um, “mind, intellect”).

parole.significato: A branch of Old Believers which is primarily known for its rejection of the ordained priesthood
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian безпоповцы (bezpopovcy) (pre-1917 spelling; modern spelling is беспоповцы (bespopovcy)). From без- (bez-) + поп (pop, “priest”) + -ов- (-ov-) + -цы (-cy) (plural of -ец (-ec)).

parole.significato: A kayak constructed by covering a light wooden frame (lashed together with sinew) in sea lion hides.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian байда́рка (bajdárka).

parole.significato: A Russian ground meat dish, often made from beef, consisting of minced meat mixed with various ingredients such as onio…
parole.testo: From Russian бифште́к(с) (bifšték(s)), from English beefsteak(s). Doublet of beefsteak and bistek.

parole.significato: A card game, a precursor to bridge.
parole.testo: From Russian бирич (birič), of obscure origin, perhaps from Turkish bir-üç (“one-three”).

parole.significato: Synonym of bitochki (“a kind of meatball from Slavic countries”).
parole.testo: From Russian битки́ (bitkí), plural of бито́к (bitók).

parole.significato: A type of round-shaped, flattened cutlets or patties, prepared from chopped meat or grains.
parole.testo: From Russian бито́чки (bitóčki), plural of бито́чек (bitóček).

parole.significato: Synonym of Antonov An-12 (“Soviet-era turboprop cargoplane”).
parole.testo: black+tulip. Calque of Russian Чёрный тюльпан (Čórnyj tjulʹpan). From the use of the aircraft as a means to repatriate corpses of fallen soldiers. parole.significato: The Soviet system of connections and social relationships; one's social or business network (in Russian or Soviet socie…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian блат (blat), from Polish blat (“cover, umbrella”) or Yiddish בלאַט (blat, “leaf, list”). Doublet of blade.

parole.significato: A blintz or blini.
parole.testo: From Russian блин (blin, “pancake, flat object”).

parole.significato: A thin Russian pancake, served stuffed with a sweet or savory filling.
parole.testo: From Russian бли́нчик (blínčik).

parole.significato: A small pancake, of Russian origin, made from buckwheat flour; traditionally served with melted butter, sour cream and…
parole.testo: From Russian блины́ (bliný), plural of блин (blin, “pancake”).

parole.significato: A type of flat pancakes made from very thin batter.
parole.testo: From Russian блинцы́ (blincý), plural of блине́ц (blinéc).

parole.significato: A whore, a bitch; a contemptible person (usually but not necessarily female).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian блядь (bljadʹ, “whore; a common expletive”).

parole.significato: An old Russian liquid measure, approximately 492 litres.
parole.testo: From Russian бо́чка (bóčka).

parole.significato: A medieval heroic warrior in Kievan Rus, akin to the Western European knight-errant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian богаты́рь (bogatýrʹ), Old East Slavic богатꙑрь (bogatyrĭ), from a Turkic language, probably Khazar, from Old Turkic [script needed] (baɣatur, “hero”), from Proto-Turkic *bagatur (“hero”). parole.significato: The head of a Russian peasant household; a family patriarch.
parole.testo: From Russian больша́к (bolʹšák).

parole.significato: A colored variation of the all-white Bolognese, a recently developed dog breed from Russia.
parole.testo: From Russian болонка (bolonka).

parole.significato: A Russian communist revolutionary, a member of the Bolshevik Party in the Communist Revolution of Russia in 1917.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian большеви́к (bolʹševík), from большинство́ (bolʹšinstvó, “majority”).

parole.significato: The strategy used by the Bolsheviks in attempting to gain power in Russia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian большеви́зм (bolʹševízm, “Bolshevism”), from большинство (bolʹšinstvo, “majority, most”) (referring to the fact that the Bolshevik faction of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party won on the majority of the important issues at the 2nd Congress of the Russian Social Democra

parole.significato: A Bolshevik.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian большевист (bolʹševist).

parole.significato: A government leftist, especially a communist, socialist, or labour union leader.
parole.testo: From Bolshevik (Russian большеви́к (bolʹševík), the socialist party in the 1918 Russian Revolution, from Russian большевики́ (bolʹševikí, “majority faction”), + -ie.

parole.significato: The study and collecting of paper money and banknotes
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian бонистики (bonistiki).

parole.significato: Synonym of Borodinsky bread.
parole.testo: Calque of Russian бороди́нский хле́б (borodínskij xléb).

parole.significato: A dark brown sourdough rye bread of Russian origin, traditionally sweetened with molasses and flavored with coriander a…
parole.testo: Partial calque of Russian бороди́нский хле́б (borodínskij xléb, literally “Borodino bread”).

parole.significato: An isometric-hexoctahedral dark gray mineral containing antimony, palladium, and tellurium.
parole.testo: Likely borrowed from Russian. Also Borovsky + -ite. Named for Igor Borisovich Borovsky.

parole.significato: A dog of a particular breed, similar in shape to a greyhound but with longer silkier hair.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian борзо́й (borzój), from бо́рзый (bórzyj, “swift”), from Proto-Indo-European *mréǵʰus (whence English brief, brace and merry).

parole.significato: A type of Slavic kvass-based cold soup.
parole.testo: From Russian ботви́нья (botvínʹja).

parole.significato: A Russian unit of measure equivalent to 1.353 pints, about the capacity of a wine bottle.
parole.testo: Russian бутылка (butylka)

parole.significato: A member of a rank of aristocracy (second only to princes) in Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Bulgaria, North Macedonia, Serb…
parole.testo: From Russian боя́ре (bojáre), plural of боя́рин (bojárin).

parole.significato: Synonym of boyardom.
parole.testo: From Russian боя́рство (bojárstvo).

parole.significato: A Russian organized crime syndicate/family.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian братва́ (bratvá, “brothers; brotherhood”). Doublet of brother.

parole.significato: Any of a certain family of trick-taking card games.
parole.testo: From the earlier game biritch, probably from Russian бирю́ч (birjúč) or бири́ч (biríč); else from Turkish bir-üç (“one-three”).

parole.significato: A type of horse-drawn carriage, with a foldable roof covering.
parole.testo: From Russian бричка (brička), or its source, Polish bryczka, diminutive form of bryka (“carriage”).

parole.significato: A traditional Eastern European bread roll, consisting of a ring of yeast-leavened wheat dough that has been boiled in w…
parole.testo: From Russian бу́блик (búblik).

parole.significato: a distinctive type of hat and an essential part of the Red Army uniform during the Russian Civil War and later
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian будёновка f (budjónovka), after Semyon Budyonny, Семён Будённый (Semjón Budjónnyj).

parole.significato: A type of self-propelled anti-aircraft missile system from the Soviet Union.
parole.testo: From Russian Бук (Buk, “codename for a missile system”), from бук (buk, “beech tree”). Doublet of beech.

parole.significato: An ancient Slavic alphabet (an adaptation of Glagolitic and Cyrillic).
parole.testo: From Russian бу́квица (búkvica).

parole.significato: A steel alloy known in Russia from medieval times.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian булат (bulat), ultimately from Persian پولاد or فولاد (“steel”).

parole.significato: An ethnonationalist ideology centered upon the revival of the Volga Bulgar identity (of which the modern Tatar, Bashkir…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian Булгари́зм (Bulgarízm). By surface analysis, Bulgar + -ism.

parole.significato: A proponent of Bulgarism.
parole.testo: Derived from Russian булгари́ст (bulgaríst), analyzable as Bulgar + -ist.

parole.significato: A soft, sweet bread roll, often filled with sweet or savory ingredients, popular in Russian and Eastern European cuisin…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian бу́лочка (búločka) and Ukrainian бу́лочка (búločka).

parole.significato: Formerly in Russia, a man employed in dragging barges or ships upstream.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian бурла́к (burlák).

parole.significato: Siberian chipmunk fur.
parole.testo: From Russian бурундук (burunduk).

parole.significato: A traditional East Slavic oral epic narrative poem.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian были́на (bylína).

parole.significato: A young boy in the Russian Empire who was taken to a special school to be trained for future compulsory military servic…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian кантонист (kantonist).

parole.significato: A phenol formaldehyde resin analogous to Bakelite used in the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian карболи́т (karbolít), from карбо́ловая кислота́ (karbólovaja kislotá, “carbolic acid”).

parole.significato: Casualties for transportation in the Soviet and modern Russian military.
parole.testo: Calque of Russian груз-200 (gruz-200), груз-две́сти (gruz-dvésti). Various theories exist regarding the Russian term.

parole.significato: A parasitic fungus of trees, usually birch, found on the circumboreal region of the Northern hemisphere, Inonotus obliq…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian ча́га (čága), Komi-Zyrian тшак (čak, “mushroom, growth”).

parole.significato: Russian tea.
parole.testo: From Russian чай (čaj, “tea”). Doublet of cha and tea.

parole.significato: A teakettle.
parole.testo: From Russian чайник (čajnik).

parole.significato: A traditional Tatar fried sweet made with honey.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian чак-ча́к (čak-čák), from Tatar чәкчәк (çäkçäk).

parole.significato: A rare mineral, ranging in color from a light lilac to a deep purple, found in Yakutia, Russia.
parole.testo: From Russian Ча́ра (Čára) (the name of a river in Siberia, Russia) + -o- + -ite.

parole.significato: A type of traditional Russian satirical or ironic folk poetry in quatrains.
parole.testo: From Russian часту́шка (častúška).

parole.significato: The letter Ч, ч.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian че (če).

parole.significato: Deep-fried turnovers filled with ground meat and onions, a national dish of the Crimean Tatars.
parole.testo: From Russian чебуре́ки (čeburéki), the plural of чебуре́к (čeburék).

parole.significato: A member of a Nakh people of the northern Caucasus and resident in the Russian republic of Chechnya.
parole.testo: From Russian чечен- (čečen-), the root in чече́нец (čečénec, “a Chechen man”) or чече́нский (čečénskij, “Chechen (adjective)”).

parole.significato: An agent of the Cheka.
parole.testo: From Russian чеки́ст (čekíst) from Чека́ (Čeká) + -ист (-ist).

parole.significato: Mari (Finno-Ugric people)

parole.significato: A Circassian.
parole.testo: From Russian черке́с (čerkés), of disputed origin, with suggestions including Turkic or Mongolic. See Circassians.

parole.significato: A major nuclear-energy accident.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian Черно́быль (Černóbylʹ). The place name is from Russian чернобыль (černobylʹ), meaning “mugwort” or “wormwood”. Doublet of Chornobyl, from the Ukrainian cognate.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian чернозём (černozjóm, “black soil”). The letter ё (jo) is usually written as е (je) in Russian, more accurately transliterated as "chernozyom"; compare чернозе́мье (černozémʹje), where ё (jo) is changed to е (je).

parole.significato: A gloomy genre of Russian horror.
parole.testo: From Russian черну́ха (černúxa), from чёрный (čórnyj, “black”).

parole.significato: Any of several former currencies of Russia: applied to various foreign gold coins prior to the reign of Peter I of Russ…
parole.testo: From Russian черво́нец (červónec), derived from черво́нное зо́лото (červónnoje zóloto), "red gold".

parole.significato: An old Russian dry measure, approximately 26.24 litres; one fourth of an osmina.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian четвери́к (četverík), from че́тверть (čétvertʹ, “quarter”) + -и́к (-ík).

parole.significato: A very strong black tea made by a special method popular in Russian prisons
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian чифир (čifir) (or чифирь (čifirʹ))

parole.significato: A warning that carries no real consequences; an empty threat.
parole.testo: Calque of Russian последнее китайское предупреждение (posledneje kitajskoje predupreždenije).

parole.significato: A minor functionary or mere bureaucrat in the Russian government.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian чиновник (činovnik).

parole.significato: A political purge in Russia.
parole.testo: From Russian чи́стка (čístka, “cleaning, purge”).

parole.significato: A shift in some Slavic languages and dialects that causes /ts/ to merge into /tʃ/.

parole.significato: The least auklet, Aethia pusilla (formerly Simorhynchus pusillus).

parole.significato: Synonym of komboskini.

parole.significato: The representation, in language, of a particular time and space.

parole.significato: A member of any of several Finnic peoples in the area of what is now Estonia, Karelia and Northwestern Russia.
parole.testo: From Russian чудь (čudʹ). Doublet of tuath.

parole.significato: Relating to or coming from Chukotka.
parole.testo: From Russian чу́кчи (čúkči), plural of чу́кча (čúkča), derived from Chukchi [script needed] (chauchu), meaning "rich in reindeer".

parole.significato: A temporary dwelling used by the nomadic Uralic reindeer herders of northwestern Siberia.
parole.testo: From Russian чум (čum), from Komi-Zyrian чум (ćum) and/or Udmurt чум (ćum, “tent, shelter”).

parole.significato: Any of several gymnastic skills created by Oksana Chusovitina and named after her.

parole.significato: From, or pertaining to, Chuvashia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian чуваш (čuvaš), see there for more.

parole.significato: An official of the Communist Party, often attached to a military unit, who was responsible for political education.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian комисса́р (komissár), from German Kommissar (“commissioner”), from Latin commissarius, from commissus, past participle of committō (“to commit, entrust to”). Doublet of commissary.

parole.significato: The process by which conflicts arise; the genesis of conflict.

parole.significato: Tending to cause conflict.
parole.testo: Ostensibly often used as a calque of Russian конфликтоге́нный (konfliktogénnyj). See also Ukrainian конфліктоге́нний (konfliktohénnyj) of identical formation.

parole.significato: Conflict resolution: the method and process involved in facilitating the peaceful ending of conflict and retribution.
parole.testo: From conflict + -ology. Rarely used in English. A calque of Russian конфликтоло́гия (konfliktológija), Ukrainian конфліктоло́гія (konfliktolóhija), Catalan conflictologia, and other language equivalents.

parole.significato: An astronaut, especially a Russian or Soviet one.

parole.significato: A loaf of fish, meat, or vegetables baked in a pastry shell.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian кулебя́ка (kulebjáka). Compare French koulibiac.

parole.significato: A type of rough linen.

parole.significato: Tarry oil of European white birch, formerly used in the arts and in medicine.

parole.significato: A participant in, or sympathizer with, the Decembrist revolt.

parole.significato: A member of the opposition faction within the Bolshevik party known as the Democratic Centralists.
parole.testo: Calque of Russian децист (decist), in turn derived from Russian демократи́ческий централи́зм (demokratíčeskij centralízm, “democratic centralism”).

parole.significato: A person who inflicts dedovshchina (a kind of hazing ritual).
parole.testo: From Russian military slang дед (ded, “soldiers after their third or fourth half-year of compulsory military service”, literally “grandfather”).

parole.significato: A Russian grandfather.

parole.significato: The representation of objects anew, in a way that we do not recognize, or that changes our reading of them.
parole.testo: From de- + familiar + -isation; possibly a calque of Russian остранение (ostranenije) as used by Russian critic Viktor Shklovsky.

parole.significato: Decembrist

parole.significato: An obsolete unit of currency in Russia equal to half a kopek.

parole.significato: A member of the Russian Airborne Troops.

parole.significato: A Russian measure of land, roughly 1.1 hectares.

parole.significato: A girl, especially one of Russian descent.

parole.significato: An old Russian unit of weight, approximately 44 milligrams.

parole.significato: An open horse-drawn carriage, especially in Russia.

parole.significato: A retinue in the service of a chieftain in mediaeval Slavic Europe.
parole.testo: From Russian дружи́на (družína, “fellowship”), from друг (drug, “companion, friend”).

parole.significato: A dead drop.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian дубо́к (dubók), from дуб (dub, “oak tree”).

parole.significato: A noncollectivized agricultural peasant in the Soviet Union.

parole.significato: The name of the letter м/М in Cyrillic alphabets.

parole.significato: The head of a group or unit of Cossacks.

parole.significato: A Socialist Revolutionary.
